title: Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful
hook: the Most Merciful, whose mercy covers everything that exists

segments.voice: Yesterday, Allah, the name itself, with no plural and ending in a breath. Your line was the name of names. Did you catch yourself hearing it inside an everyday phrase? Day two hundred thirty-five.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions are camped at Hudaybiyyah, outside Mecca, and a peace treaty is being written with the Quraysh, the people who drove them out. Ali holds the pen. The Prophet dictates the first words: bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. And the Meccan envoy, Suhayl, stops him. As for ar-Rahman, he says, by God, I don't know what that is. Write in Your name, O Allah, the way you used to. The companions bristle. It's the first line of the treaty, and it's already a fight. What happens next says something about the name itself. Today: Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful.
screen: `A TREATY AT HUDAYBIYYAH.` → `ALI HOLDS THE PEN.` → `I DON'T KNOW WHAT AR-RAHMAN IS.`

segments.voice: The Prophet said: write it as he asks. Bismika Allahumma. In Your name, O Allah. Bukhari records it. The name of mercy gave way so that peace could be written, and some readers see mercy itself in that. Why didn't Suhayl know the name? The report doesn't say, but the Qur'an records Meccans asking the same thing: and what is ar-Rahman? It comes from the root r-h-m, the root of mercy, and its form, fa'lan, is one that grammarians say Arabic uses for things that are full, overflowing, at their peak, like ghadban, full of anger, or 'atshan, full of thirst. So ar-Rahman is mercy at its fullest, mercy that fills everything. Scholars say the name belongs to Allah alone; no person is to be called ar-Rahman. And the Qur'an gives it an entire surah. Surah ar-Rahman opens with the name alone, and then lists gifts: the Qur'an taught, speech, the sun and moon in their courses, fruit, the palm with its sheaths, grain, the two seas. Thirty-one times it asks, which of the favors of your Lord will you deny? Here is how the Qur'an puts it in Surah al-A'raf, in Pickthall's translation: and My mercy embraceth all things. All things. One classical explanation reads ar-Rahman as mercy that reaches every creature in this world, whoever they are, whatever they believe: the rain falls on every field. The name's closer partner comes tomorrow.
screen: `WRITE IT AS HE ASKS.` · `WHAT IS AR-RAHMAN?` · `FA'LAN — FULL, OVERFLOWING.` · `MY MERCY EMBRACETH ALL THINGS.` · then, large: `MERCY COVERS ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit, and open your eyes softly. For one minute, look for mercy. Not the dramatic kind. The light coming through a window. The chair holding you up. The air arriving in your lungs without being asked. Your heart doing its work while you weren't paying attention. Name each one silently as you find it. Then close your eyes and let the list keep going on its own. If you pray, you can say, ya Rahman, softly, at the end. The bell holds the time.
Ar-Rahman. The Most Merciful, mercy at its fullest, overflowing onto everything that exists, a name used only for Allah. Today's word.
Your line: mercy covers all. Today, when you're tempted to think someone is outside of every mercy, remember the rain falling on every field. Day two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims say ar-Rahman in every bismillah, and Surah ar-Rahman, with its refrain about the favors of the Lord, is often recited; Abdul-Rahman, servant of the Most Merciful, is a common name.

fork.setup: the treaty's first line is disputed: the envoy won't accept ar-Rahman. you're the Prophet. what do you do?
options: have it written: in Your name, O Allah
fork.reveal: he told Ali to write bismika Allahumma (Bukhari). the name of mercy gave way so peace could be written.

original.note: Arabic: the Most Merciful, mercy at its fullest; from r-h-m.

trapdoor: what you thought: another way of saying God is kind.
what it means: mercy at its fullest, overflowing onto everything that exists, a name for Allah alone.
what a scholar hears: the fa'lan form marks fullness; 25:60, what is ar-Rahman?; Bukhari 2731 at Hudaybiyyah; 7:156, mercy embraces all things.

sources.quoted: and My mercy embraceth all things,

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731–2732 (the treaty of Hudaybiyyah and the basmala)

notes: Please confirm Pickthall's wording of the phrase in 7:156.
Bukhari 2731–2732 cited from memory; confirm the details (Ali as scribe, Suhayl's words).
The count of thirty-one refrains in Surah ar-Rahman should be confirmed.
The fa'lan-form explanation is a standard grammatical gloss; the reading of ar-Rahman as mercy for all creation in this world is one common view.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the year 628 from hook and screen (not in the cited report); Suhayl's reason no longer asserted, only the Qur'an's 'what is ar-Rahman?'; fa'lan, exclusivity and the 'rain on every field' reading now attributed to grammarians/scholars; dropped 'among the most loved surahs'. Keeper: Bukhari 2731 names 'the scribe'; Ali is named in other versions (e.g. Bukhari 2699, Muslim 1783).
